goal_alignment.note: phases/writing/draft_1.md answers all four campaign questions. Q1 seasonality is Figure 1, Q2 day-of-week/hour and commute peaks are Figures 2-3, Q3 member vs casual is Figures 4-5, and the optional Q4 weather is Figures 6-7. It states the data source, the cleaning rules with counts, and the limitations (one city, rider-type definition, provenance, one-point weather proxy). Findings are worded as associations, and causation is explicitly disclaimed (summary, Interpretation bullet, weather section). It follows the analysis-phase advice to describe a summer-autumn plateau rather than a single peak month. It is on the long side for a 'short report' (about 140 lines, 7 figures, a hypotheses table), but the four findings are clear.

completeness.note: The draft has an executive summary, data and methods, results for four findings, a hypotheses table, limitations and reproducibility. It includes 8 PNGs, 7 of which are referenced. The cleaning table has one row per rule with counts, and every analysis-phase recommendation (provenance caveat, DST artefact for R3, R5 asymmetry, casual has no distinct AM peak, e-bike confound, autocorrelated weather residuals) is carried over. Gaps: (1) Figure 2's 2024 panel clips the weekday 17:00 peak and its '08:00' label collides with the legend, and Figure 1 panel A has overlapping 'trough Jan' / 'trough Feb' labels. I confirmed both by viewing the PNGs. The draft discloses both defects, but they are fixable by regenerating the plots in /app/code/03_temporal_analysis.py and were not fixed. (2) fig_hourly_seasonal_robustness.png is shipped but not referenced or checked, which is clutter. The weekday/weekend plot is the main evidence for the commute-peak finding, so shipping it clipped is the main blemish.

correctness.note: I spot-checked the numbers against /app/output/tables and they match. cleaning_summary.csv gives 38,596 of 79,410,195 removed (0.0486%) and 79,371,599 kept, and the per-rule counts 643 / 182 / 37,576 / 195 sum to 38,596. Per-year R5 is 26,640 vs 10,936. peak_hours.csv gives AM 08:00 and PM 17:00 at 100% agreement, AM/midday 1.46 and 1.54, PM/midday 1.97 and 2.04, and weekend 15:00 at 96% and 73%. seasonality_peak_trough.csv gives total-based ratios 2.34 and 2.73, per-day 2.21 (2.07-2.42) and 2.74 (2.49-3.14), and peak-month agreement 0.55-0.88. member_casual_summary.csv gives weekend shares 23.3/35.3 (2023) and 23.8/35.6 (2024), and median durations 8.55/13.84 and 8.35/13.10. member_casual_peak_hours.csv supports 'casual 2023 weekday AM not distinct (agreement 0.65)'. Winter share is 16.2%/14.3% and Jun-Oct is 52.0%/54.8%. The 2024/2023 monthly ratio ranges 1.05-1.44. weather_models.csv gives rain effects -9.0/-23.4/-42.1%, temperature +38.2% per 10C from 10 to 20C and +10.6% (CI 3.1-18.5) from 20 to 30C, and +3.69% per C (2.97-4.41) with month fixed effects. pbin counts 367+180+90+94 = 731. The claim that all four DST dates are Sundays is true. The figures I viewed (Figures 1, 2, 4, 6) match the text. Minor inconsistencies: the executive summary says 35.4% for casual weekend share in 2023 while the table and source say 35.3% (0.3535); the executive summary quotes casual peak/trough 4.4-5.4 (monthly totals) while the Section 3 table gives 3.9/5.5 (per-day) without saying the basis differs; the rain Spearman rho is -0.2845, which rounds to -0.28, not -0.29. None of these changes a conclusion.

traceability.note: Every number maps to a named table or script under /app/output/tables and /app/code (01_acquire.py ... 04_weather.py). Methods name the bootstrap settings (2,000 resamples, seed 20240501), the Newey-West lag (7), the weather source (Open-Meteo, Central Park, weather_source.json) and the raw-file manifest (data_manifest.json). The 2023 provenance caveat (yearly zip, monthly URLs 404) is stated openly. The claim that an independent re-query reproduced the 24 monthly counts, clean total and peak hours is carried from the analysis-phase verdict, and I did not rerun it, but the numbers I checked agree with the tables. The hypothesis 'confidence' values (0.93, 0.90, ...) are the pipeline's subjective scores, not statistics, and are not labelled as such in the draft.

summary: The report is sound to finalize. It answers all four questions from real 2023-2024 NYC Citi Bike data (79.37M trips kept, 0.049% removed, each rule reported), and every number I spot-checked matches /app/output/tables. Uncertainty is shown with bootstrap CIs, the unstable peak month is described honestly as a plateau, the weather result is framed as association only, and limitations are thorough and candid. The weaknesses are presentational: the 2024 panel of the key weekday/weekend hourly figure clips the 17:00 peak, the monthly figure has overlapping labels, and there are three small rounding/basis inconsistencies in the text. These do not affect the conclusions, and they are disclosed in the draft, so I am not sending it back.
recommendations: Regenerate fig_hourly_weekday_vs_weekend.png with a shared y-limit above about 12.5k (or a per-panel limit) so the 2024 weekday 17:00 peak is visible, and move the legend off the '08:00' label. Remove the 'Known plot defect' note from the Figure 2 caption afterwards.

Fix the overlapping 'trough Jan 1.89M' / 'trough Feb 1.69M' labels in panel A of fig_monthly_volume.png (offset them or label only one trough per year), and remove the matching sentence from the Limitations section.

Make the numbers consistent: use 35.3% (not 35.4%) for casual weekend share in 2023 in the executive summary; use rho = -0.28 for the rain Spearman correlation (source -0.2845); and say in the executive summary and the Section 3 table whether casual/member peak/trough is on monthly totals (4.4-5.4 / 2.1-2.5) or per day (3.9-5.5 / 2.0-2.5).
Either remove fig_hourly_seasonal_robustness.png from the deliverable or view it and reference it, since it is currently shipped unchecked.
Label the confidence values in the 'Hypotheses and outcomes' table as subjective analyst scores, or drop them. Consider trimming that table to keep the report 'short' as the brief asks.

If time allows, check the 2023 yearly zip against any monthly 2023 file, and look at what the >24 h (R5) trips are in 2023. These are the only unresolved data-provenance items, and the draft already states both as limitations.
